## TL;DR

Cross-process slot `.heartbeat.json` / `.started.json` ages were computed by
subtracting the writer process's `process.hrtime` reading from the reader
process's, which is meaningless across processes: Bun's `process.hrtime` is
relative to process start while Node's is system uptime. A server watchdog that
had been up for hours therefore computed roughly its own uptime as the holder's
heartbeat age, escalated healthy checks as `needs_input` / check-wait, and the
same math fed stale-slot reclaim, so a waiting check could terminate a live
holder and exceed `heavySlots`. The fix makes cross-process ages wall-clock
based, keeps monotonic comparison only for timestamps written by the current
process, records the writer PID in both timestamp files, and adds regression
tests for age reporting, old-wall-clock stall detection, live-slot reclaim, and
the watchdog escalation. `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passes.

## Work and rationale

The root cause was in `src/core/cross-process-slots.ts`. Writers stored
`{ wallMs, monotonicMs }` in `.heartbeat.json` and `.started.json`; readers
ignored `wallMs` and did `monotonicMs() - heartbeat.monotonicMs`. That is safe
only inside one process. Under Bun a fresh process reports a monotonic value
near zero, while the long-running server reports hours, so `Math.max(0,
reader - writer)` produced the server's own uptime and flagged every check as
silent. Under Node both readings share a system-uptime origin, which is why the
bug was invisible there and only reproduced under the default Bun runtime.

I introduced a single parsing/aging seam instead of patching each reader:

- `readSlotTimestamp()` parses `wallMs`, `monotonicMs`, and the new writer
  `pid` defensively (non-finite and non-integer values are ignored).
- `slotTimestampAgeMs()` uses the monotonic delta only when the timestamp's
  `pid` equals `process.pid`; otherwise it uses `Date.now() - wallMs`. If a
  file has neither usable field it returns `undefined`, and callers keep the
  existing directory-mtime fallback. That preserves the old compatibility path
  for pre-fix or hand-written slot directories.
- Writers now include `pid: process.pid` and use one `Date.now()` for both
  started and heartbeat in `tryTakeSlot`, plus the PID in the periodic
  heartbeat.

Both readers now go through that helper: `isStaleSlot()` (which feeds
`tryTakeSlot`, `countActiveSlots`, and therefore reclaim) and
`inspectCrossProcessSlots()` (which feeds the watchdog, the Checks surface,
`repoos check --slots`, and driver briefs). Using one helper is important
because the false `needs_input` escalation and the live-slot reclaim were two
symptoms of one calculation; fixing only the watchdog would have left reclaim
able to kill a live holder.

The same-process monotonic shortcut is intentional: it keeps the existing
protection against wall-clock/directory-time jumps (for example NTP steps or
sandbox clock changes) for a process inspecting its own heartbeat. The
`pid` field is what makes that distinction possible without guessing. I updated
the two existing tests that exercised clock-jump protection and wedge timing to
include `pid: process.pid`, and changed the process-group termination fixture
to use an old `wallMs` with the child's PID, because that heartbeat is
cross-process by construction.

I also added a short paragraph to `docs/architecture.md` under the Runtime
section recording the Bun-vs-Node `process.hrtime` difference and the rule:
persisted monotonic values may only be compared by the process that wrote them;
cross-process ages use the wall clock or file mtime. I also grepped every other
`process.hrtime` use in `src/`. The integration orchestrator uses it for
in-process elapsed timing, and `budgetMonotonicStartNs` is intended for the
same close-out process; I left that out of scope, but the new docs rule is the
checklist for auditing it if close-out jobs ever outlive their server process.

Tests added in `src/ui-app/tests/local-resource-gates.test.ts`:

1. A cross-process heartbeat with a near-zero monotonic value and a current
   `wallMs` reports an age under five seconds, not the reader's uptime. The
   reader's `process.hrtime.bigint` is stubbed to ~100 minutes so the old code
   would deterministically report a stall.
2. A cross-process heartbeat whose `wallMs` is 31 minutes old is still reported
   wedged with `heartbeatAgeMs` and `ageMs` at or above 30 minutes.
3. A live child process holding a slot with a fresh wall-clock heartbeat is not
   reclaimed: `acquireCrossProcessSlot` times out, the directory remains, and
   the child is still alive. Under the old math the same setup killed the child
   and stole the slot.

`src/ui-app/tests/task-watchdog.test.ts` adds the acceptance-criterion-4 case:
a 15-minute queue wait behind a live holder with a fresh heartbeat written by a
different PID does not set `needsInput` or `needsInputReason`, and the queue
marker stays visible as a normal wait. The watchdog's reader path is the real
`inspectCrossProcessSlots`, so this covers the production wiring rather than a
mock.

## Approaches tried

The first instinct was to prefer `wallMs` unconditionally and delete
`monotonicMs`. That is the smallest fix, but it removes the clock-jump
protection an existing test explicitly covers. Keeping same-PID monotonic
comparison preserves both: cross-process ages use the wall clock, and a process
reading its own heartbeat still uses monotonic time.

I considered using the slot directory mtime as the only age source. It is
cross-process by nature, but `utimesSync` is a separate step from the heartbeat
write and older directories do not refresh it consistently. `wallMs` is written
with the heartbeat content, so it is the better primary source, with mtime as
the fallback.

For the tests I considered spawning a real Bun child to write the heartbeat,
but that adds process-start and filesystem timing noise and still may not create
a large reader uptime in a short run. Stubbing `process.hrtime.bigint` on the
reader reproduces the broken arithmetic deterministically under either runtime,
while the heartbeat still claims a different `pid`. The existing suite already
uses PID fixtures and child process groups, so this fits its style.

## Challenges and blockers

The first scoped `repoos check` timed out in the `build` step after 120
seconds while the UI build was running under load. `repoos stats` showed a
pressure warning (available memory 26%, one heavy job running). Re-running just
`repoos check --step build` passed in 37 seconds, and the full scoped check then
passed with the build taking 261ms. This was machine/load timing, not a source
failure; no code change was made in response.

The pre-existing tests encoded the old assumption in their fixtures. The
clock-jump test wrote `wallMs: 0` and relied on monotonic; that is correct only
for the same process, so adding `pid: process.pid` keeps its intent. The wedged
process-group test wrote a monotonic-only heartbeat for a child PID; under the
new rule that is cross-process data, so it now uses an old `wallMs` and the
child's PID. Updating the fixtures made the rule explicit rather than weakening
the assertions.

## Key learnings

- A monotonic clock is not a cross-process clock. Bun's `process.hrtime`
  origin differs from Node's, and both differ from any other process's origin
  under Bun. Persist a wall clock, or persist the writer identity with the
  monotonic value and only compare inside that process.
- One bad age calculation can have two very different consequences. Here it
  produced false human-input escalations and also authorized reclaim of a live
  slot, which is a capacity-safety bug. Route both through one helper and test
  both consumers.
- When a test's clock semantics mirror the bug, update the fixture to state the
  intended semantics explicitly (here, which PID wrote the timestamp) rather
  than removing the protection the test was written for.
